African American Vernacular English, or AAVE, is a variety of English spoken by many African Americans with roots in the complex linguistic history of African languages, English, and creolization during slavery. It is a fully systematic dialect with distinctive phonology, grammar, and vocabulary. Though historically stigmatized, it is linguistically valid and has emerged as an important marker of cultural identity.

One of the most distinctive features is invariant be to mark habitual action. When someone says "He be studyin'" they mean "He studies regularly," quite different from "He is studyin'" in standard English. Another key feature is the deletion of auxiliary verbs. Instead of "Are you going?" speakers might say "You going?" and instead of "I'm going to go" they say "I'ma go."

AAVE speakers also reduce consonant clusters by dropping final consonants, so "test" becomes "tes" and "cold" becomes "col." The word "ain't" serves as a general negative covering both past and present, as in "I ain't seen it." Phonologically, vowel distinctions before the r sound reduce, so Carol, coral, and barrel may sound alike.

There has been vigorous debate among linguists about whether AAVE descends primarily from West African languages, English dialects, or creolization, but linguists recognize it as a fully systematic rule-governed variety. It shares regional roots and some phonological features with Southern American English and has been measured unfairly against General American, the prestige American standard, despite its grammatical coherence. It may possibly descend from creole languages through earlier creolization during and after slavery.
